title: Sagas & Distributed Transactions
subtitle: Watch one order touch three services, see why a global lock breaks, and see how a saga undoes work instead.
learn: Why two-phase commit (2PC) blocks and why most microservice teams avoid it
How a saga replaces one big transaction with a chain of small local ones
The difference between orchestration and choreography, and when each fits
How compensating actions undo earlier steps, and why they must be idempotent and retried
What a saga cannot give you: isolation between concurrent sagas

steps.title: One order, three databases
steps.body: A customer places one order. Behind the scenes that means three separate jobs: charge the card (Payment database), reserve the item (Inventory database) and book a courier (Shipping database). Each service owns its own database, so no single BEGIN ... COMMIT (one transaction where all changes succeed or none do) can cover all three. The animation shows the order arriving at the Order service. The worry: what if the card is charged but the courier booking fails? This lesson shows how to keep the three writes consistent without one shared transaction.
steps.idea: Once data is split across services, one ACID transaction (all-or-nothing, consistent, isolated, durable) can no longer cover the whole business action.
steps.caption: One order must change data in three services, each with its own database.

steps.title: The classic answer: two-phase commit
steps.body: Two-phase commit (2PC) is the classic fix. A coordinator, here the Order service, runs two rounds. Round one: it asks every participant to PREPARE, meaning do the work, lock the rows and promise it can commit. Round two: if all answer YES it sends COMMIT, otherwise ABORT. The animation shows three PREPAREs, three YES votes, then three COMMITs. The result is all-or-nothing, but the rows stay locked the whole time. With 5 ms round trips it takes roughly 10 to 20 ms; we use 15 ms.
steps.idea: 2PC gives all-or-nothing results, but every participant must hold its locks until the coordinator decides.
steps.caption: Votes are collected, then COMMIT is sent, and locks are held the whole time.

steps.title: Why 2PC hurts at scale
steps.body: What if the coordinator crashes after the YES votes arrive but before it sends its decision? Every participant is stuck. It promised it could commit, so it cannot abort alone, and it keeps its locks. An operator can force a guess, but that risks inconsistent data. Say the restart takes 30 seconds: for that long, other orders touching those rows wait in line. Even without a crash, one slow participant stalls everyone. And a card processor does not speak XA, the standard 2PC protocol for databases, so across independent services and third-party APIs 2PC is rarely an option.
steps.idea: 2PC blocks on coordinator failure, and it is a poor fit across independently owned services and third-party APIs.
steps.caption: The coordinator is down and three services are stuck holding locks.

steps.title: The saga idea
steps.body: A saga drops the global lock. It splits the job into a chain of small local transactions, one per service. Each commits right away and releases its locks. If a later step fails, the saga runs a compensating action (a new action that reverses the business effect, like a refund) for every step already done. While it runs, the data is briefly inconsistent; it becomes consistent once the saga finishes (eventual consistency). You give up atomicity and isolation to stay available. Assume 10 ms per step and a 3 ms lock. The animation shows step one: Payment charges $40 and commits.
steps.idea: A saga is a series of local commits, each with a planned undo, giving eventual consistency instead of atomicity.
steps.caption: Payment commits on its own and frees its lock after about 3 ms.

steps.title: Orchestration: a conductor drives it
steps.body: In an orchestrated saga, one component holds the workflow. Here it is the Order service: it tells each service what to do and waits for the answer. Payment is already charged. The animation shows the orchestrator telling Inventory to reserve the item (done), then telling Shipping to book a courier, which is still in progress. The order of steps and the failure rules live in one place, often a saved state machine, so the saga can resume after a crash. Each service just does its local job and replies.
steps.idea: Orchestration keeps the saga's flow in one place that tells each service what to do next.
steps.caption: The orchestrator commands each step in turn and waits for the reply.

steps.title: A step fails: run the undo steps
steps.body: Shipping finds no courier and reports failure. Its own transaction rolled back, so there is nothing to undo there. The orchestrator walks backwards: it releases the reserved stock, then refunds the $40. These are new forward actions, not database rollbacks, because those steps already committed. Tip: put steps likely to fail early and hard-to-undo steps late, after the pivot (the go/no-go step). Here Shipping fails last, so a real design might book the courier first, or only authorize the card and capture it at the pivot, so an early failure is a quiet void, not a visible refund. If a reply times out, treat the result as unknown and compensate anyway.
steps.idea: Compensating actions are new transactions that reverse committed steps, run in reverse order.
steps.caption: No courier: the saga releases the stock, then refunds the payment.

steps.title: Choreography: services react to events
steps.body: The alternative has no conductor. The Order service publishes an OrderPlaced event on the event bus (a shared message channel). Payment hears it, charges, and publishes PaymentTaken. Inventory hears that, reserves stock and publishes StockReserved, and Shipping reacts to that. Each service only knows which events it listens to and which it emits. There is no central coordinator to fail, though the bus itself must stay highly available. Adding a listener changes nothing else, but nobody holds the whole flow. Each bus hop adds about 5 ms, so the six hops shown take about 30 ms.
steps.idea: Choreography encodes the saga as a chain of events, with no central coordinator and no single place that shows the whole flow.
steps.caption: Each event passes the baton to the next service through the bus.

steps.title: Choosing between the two
steps.body: Choreography handles failure too. Shipping emits ShipFailed, Inventory hears it and releases stock, and Payment reacts to that by refunding. (Payment could also listen to ShipFailed directly.) As a rule of thumb, choreography suits short sagas of two to four steps with few owners, because it is simple and loosely coupled. Beyond that, the event chain is hard to follow and circular dependencies creep in, so orchestration pays off: one place to read, test, time out and monitor. Its cost is one more component to run, and it can attract business logic, so keep it to sequencing.
steps.idea: Choreography wins on coupling for small flows; orchestration wins on visibility once flows grow or branch.
steps.caption: Choreographed failure: ShipFailed, then stock released, then refund.

steps.title: Retries, duplicates, and dirty reads
steps.body: Messages are usually delivered at least once, so duplicates happen. Every step and compensation must be idempotent (safe to run twice, with the same result). The animation sends refund #881 twice, and Payment answers 'already done' the second time because each command carries a saga and step ID. Retry compensations with backoff, and alert a human if one cannot succeed. Save the local change and the outgoing message in one local transaction (a transactional outbox) so a crash cannot lose the next step. Because each step is visible once committed, mark in-progress data with a PENDING flag (a semantic lock).
steps.idea: Sagas need idempotent steps and explicit handling of half-finished state, because they give no isolation.
steps.caption: The duplicate refund command is ignored.

steps.title: Atomic, or available
steps.body: 2PC gives atomic commits across services, but it blocks if the coordinator fails and holds locks, so it is rare between microservices. A saga gives up atomicity and isolation: each local transaction commits, and a failure triggers compensations in reverse order. Use orchestration for longer or branching flows and choreography for short ones. Make every step idempotent, and plan for the in-between states.
steps.idea: Replace one big lock with small commits and planned undo steps, and design for the in-between.
steps.caption: Local commits plus compensations when something fails.

quiz.q: A 2PC coordinator crashes after all participants voted YES but before it sent COMMIT. What is the main problem?
options: Participants abort immediately and the order is lost
Participants keep their locks and wait for a decision
Participants commit by themselves after a short timeout
The vote results are replayed from the event bus
quiz.why: Having voted YES, a participant promised it can commit and cannot safely abort or commit without the decision, so it blocks while holding locks.

quiz.q: In a saga, the payment step has committed and shipping then reports that no courier is available. What is the correct recovery?
options: Roll back the payment database transaction
Retry shipping forever and leave payment as is
Run a compensating action such as a refund
Delete the payment row directly from the Payment DB
quiz.why: The payment transaction already committed and released its locks, so it cannot be rolled back. A new forward action, the refund, reverses its business effect.

quiz.q: Your saga has seven steps with conditional branches and the team keeps losing track of where an order is stuck. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to choreography so each service owns less
Use 2PC for the last three steps of the flow
Remove every compensation to simplify the flow
Orchestrate it with a stored workflow state
quiz.why: Orchestration puts the flow and its current state in one place, which makes long or branching sagas readable, testable, and monitorable.

quiz.q: A refund command is delivered twice because of a retry. Why is that safe in a well-built saga?
options: The event bus guarantees exactly-once delivery everywhere
The refund is idempotent, keyed by saga and step ID
Sagas hold a global lock during compensation
Retries are disabled during compensation
quiz.why: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen, so each step and compensation must detect a repeat via an idempotency key and do nothing the second time.

quiz.q: While one order's saga is mid-flight, a second request reads the last item as reserved, but that saga may still fail and release it. Which tool reduces this problem?
options: Hold row locks in all three databases until the saga ends
Retry compensations faster
A bigger event bus
Mark the item PENDING (a semantic lock) so others know it is mid-saga
quiz.why: Sagas commit each step early and give no isolation, so other requests can see half-finished state. A semantic lock such as a PENDING flag tells them the reservation may still be undone, so they can wait, warn, or treat it as uncertain. Holding cross-database locks for the whole saga is exactly the blocking that sagas avoid.

cheatsheet.def: Coordinator asks all participants to PREPARE, then COMMIT or ABORT. Atomic, but blocking and lock-heavy.
A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action, giving eventual consistency across services.
A central orchestrator sends commands to each step and owns the flow and failure rules. Better for long flows.
Services react to each other's events with no central coordinator. Loosely coupled, but the flow is implicit.
A new transaction that semantically undoes a committed step, such as a refund. Run in reverse order and retried until it succeeds.
An ID sent with each command so a duplicate delivery is recognised and ignored.
A status flag like PENDING that marks data as mid-saga so other requests treat it carefully.
The go/no-go step of a saga. Steps before it are compensatable; once it commits, the saga is committed to finishing, and later steps are retried until they succeed.
